lesson.title: The Article Grid & the ein-Family
lesson.subtitle: der/the, das/that, dieser/this, mein/mine — one ancient demonstrative system

payoff.text: That D is back. der, die and das all begin with the hardened TH of 'the' — the shift you met in topic 4, doing its second job. Every German article is D- plus the pronoun that would replace the noun.

hook.title: The Is a Demonstrative in Disguise
hook.content: English speakers feel that German articles are arbitrary. They are not: der, die, das are the same ancient demonstrative word that gave English the — and its cousins that and this. Das ist mein Haus says 'That is mine house', and every word is a twin: das ↔ that, ist ↔ is, mein ↔ mine (the King James Bible still says 'mine eyes'). The ein-family — ein, kein, mein, dein — is one grid with one behavior, and kein is literally 'not one', the same construction as English none.

footnotes.title: The That/Das Doublet
footnotes.content: Both English that and German das descend from Proto-Germanic *þat — the neuter of the ancient demonstrative. Old English had sē/sēo/þæt ('the/that'); the article and the demonstrative were one word doing two jobs, and German simply never split them apart.

pattern.title: The Grid and the Family
pattern.content: Read the grid as one decomposition instead of three memorised words: der = D- + er (he), die = D- + sie (she/they), das = D- + es (it), and dieser = dies- + er for pointing close. The ein-family declines as one word: ein → einen (topic 10's Him-Case), and kein and mein copy it exactly. Before das Haus: das ist mein Haus, ich habe kein Haus. Before der Kaffee as an object: ich trinke keinen Kaffee — the full Him-Case, -en and all. Before die Zeit: ich habe keine Zeit. Every family member marches in step: ein, kein, mein, dein — same endings, same grid, because they are all the same demonstrative doing the same job.
pattern.linguist_note: mein ↔ mine is exact: Proto-Germanic *mīnaz. English later reduced unstressed mine to my before nouns ('my house') while German kept the full form — the KJV's 'mine eyes have seen' is the older system both languages once shared.

exercises.prompt: Match the demonstrative and possessive twins:
exercises.target_answer: dieser, das, mein, kein, mein Bett, der Stuhl, der Löffel
exercises.meaning: this, that, my/mine, no, my bed, the chair, the spoon
exercises.explanation: One ancient demonstrative system split across two languages — and the room words slot into it: das ist mein Bett, der Stuhl ist neu.

exercises.prompt: Complete: 'Ich habe _____ Teller' (with the possessive, accusative):
exercises.meaning: Ich habe meinen Teller = I have my plate
exercises.explanation: mein copies ein exactly: masculine accusative adds -en (the Him-Case): der Teller → meinen Teller.

exercises.prompt: Negate the possession: 'Ich habe _____ Zeit' (kein + feminine die Zeit):
exercises.meaning: Ich habe keine Zeit = I have no time
exercises.explanation: kein declines like ein: before die Zeit it takes -e. English none is the same 'not one' construction.

exercises.prompt: What older English possessive is the exact twin of 'mein'?
exercises.explanation: Both descend from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz. 'Mine eyes' in the KJV is mein's living English relative.

exercises.idea: you're showing someone around your new room: point at the window and say that is my window
cues: Every word is a twin: das ↔ that, ist ↔ is, mein ↔ mine
Pointing word first, verb second, then what's yours: Das ist mein Fenster
exercises.explanation: One sentence, four cognates — the demonstrative system you already spoke in King James English, now pointing at a window.

summary.outcome: Use dieser, mein, and kein with correct endings across the ein-family grid.
summary.takeaway: der/die/das and the/that/this are one demonstrative system; ein, kein, mein, dein decline as one family.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the article gym — twenty nouns, three colors: rapid der/die/das reps with every table noun.

twist.prompt: Same grid, new job — negate the noun: I have no time. (kein declines exactly like ein.)
twist.explanation: Zeit is feminine, so kein wears its feminine dress: keine. nicht is for verbs — nouns get the 'not one' word. You just negated without a not.

die.etymology_derivation: th → d. Sounds identical to emphatic English "thee".

das.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
das.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and final t → s.

dieser.etymology_derivation: North Sea Germanic demonstrative: Old English þis and German dieser are one system — dies- ↔ this. [wiktionary]

mein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mīnaz — identical to English mine; the KJV's 'mine eyes' preserves the older use. [wiktionary]

kein.etymology_derivation: Back-formation of nekein 'not any' (ni + ein, 'not one') — built right on ein, exactly like English none ← 'not one'. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

bett.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *badją — explicitly cognate with English bed; the High German d→t gives the final -tt. [wiktionary]

teller.etymology_derivation: From Middle French tailloir, meaning cutting board, from the Old French cutting verb tailler; English tailor descends from the same Old French verb. [wiktionary]

stuhl.context_translation: The chair stands at the table.
stuhl.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stōl — cognate with English stool; the meaning narrowed from stool to chair. [wiktionary]

fenster.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fenestr, an early borrowing of Latin fenestra — a Latin loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

löffel.context_phrase: Nimm einen Löffel für die Suppe.
löffel.context_translation: Take a spoon for the soup.
löffel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic lapilaz, from the root lap, meaning to lick or lap; English lap is the related word, and its p appears as f in German. [wiktionary]

setzen.context_phrase: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
setzen.context_translation: I sit down on the chair.
setzen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, a causative of sit; the page documents cognate English set. The t of set reappears as z (ts) in setzen, the same sibilant shift as two and zwei. [wiktionary]

sitzen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
sitzen.context_translation: We are sitting in the café.

halten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *haldaną — English hold is the documented cognate; German hardened d to t (the stop shift). Strong verb, class 7: hielt, gehalten. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
